questions.stem: Your team is building an electricity substation next to a primary school. Over the past fortnight the head teacher has phoned the site foreman six times about lorry deliveries at drop-off time, and has been given three different answers. The communications management plan lists the client, the local authority and the utility, but not the school. What should you do?

options.text: Ask the foreman to refer any further calls from the head teacher to you, so that the school hears one consistent answer from the project from now on.
options.rationale: This fixes the inconsistency but not the gap. The school still has to phone to find anything out, and the candidate has treated a missing stakeholder as a problem of who answers the phone.

options.text: Add the school to the communications management plan with a named project contact and a weekly notice of deliveries planned around drop-off and pick-up times.
options.rationale: Six calls in a fortnight show a stakeholder with a continuing information need that nobody owns. Planning for it gives the school one voice, a known contact and information before it has to ask.

options.text: Write to the head teacher with an apology and the full delivery schedule for the remaining eight months, and ask the school to contact you if anything changes.
options.rationale: A one-off letter goes out of date as soon as the schedule moves. The candidate has chosen a single push message for a need that continues for the life of the works.

options.text: Raise the school's concerns at the next liaison meeting with the local authority, which represents residents and community bodies on matters affecting the project.
options.rationale: This routes a direct, practical need through a proxy that does not run the school day. The candidate assumes an existing stakeholder can stand in for one the plan left out.

questions.explanation: Anyone affected enough by a project to keep asking about it belongs in the communications plan, with a defined owner, content and frequency. Repeated ad hoc enquiries are the signal that a stakeholder has been missed, and the fix is to plan for that stakeholder rather than to get better at answering each enquiry as it arrives.
questions.mindset: Treat a stakeholder who keeps asking as a gap in the plan, not an interruption.

questions.stem: After your claims-processing team moved to hybrid working, its wall board was replaced by a board in an online tool. The operations manager, who used to glance at the wall each morning, has asked the team to email him a daily summary of what is in progress and what is blocked. The team estimates this will take 20 minutes a day. What should you do?

options.text: Give the operations manager access to the online board with a saved view of in-progress and blocked items, and spend ten minutes showing him how to read it.
options.rationale: He has lost a view he used to have, not asked for new information. Restoring that view in the new tool meets the need at almost no ongoing cost and keeps the board as the single source.

options.text: Agree to the daily email for now, rotating the task around the team so that no single person carries the twenty minutes on every day of the week.
options.rationale: Rotation spreads the cost but keeps it. The candidate has accepted a push report as the answer without checking whether the information is already available to pull.

options.text: Invite the operations manager to attend the team's daily stand-up, where he will hear what is in progress and blocked directly from the people doing the work.
options.rationale: The stand-up is the team's planning event, and an observer who wants status tends to turn it into a report to him. It also costs him more time than a glance at the board did.

options.text: Ask the product owner to include in-progress and blocked items in the fortnightly sprint review summary that is already sent to the operations team.
options.rationale: A fortnightly summary cannot meet a daily need. The candidate has reused an existing channel without checking that its frequency matches what the reader actually uses the information for.

questions.explanation: When an information radiator moves online, the people who read it in passing lose access without anyone deciding that they should. The first response to a request for a report is to check whether the information already exists in a form the requester can pull for themselves. A push report built to replace a lost view creates a standing cost for something the team already produces.
questions.mindset: Before producing a new report, ask whether the reader can simply see what the team already sees.

questions.stem: Attendance at your mobile banking app's sprint reviews has fallen from twelve business stakeholders to three over the last four sprints. The reviews run for an hour every second Thursday and follow the same format as when attendance was high. The product owner wants to ask the sponsor to make attendance compulsory for the named stakeholders. What should you do first?

options.text: Shorten the review to thirty minutes and open with the items each stakeholder group requested, so that the time they spend there is visibly worth it.
options.rationale: This is a sensible redesign chosen without knowing the cause. If the stakeholders stopped because their input was not acted on, a shorter review will not bring them back.

options.text: Speak to several of the stakeholders who stopped coming to find out what changed for them, before deciding what about the review needs to change.
options.rationale: The review has not changed, so something changed for its audience. Asking separates causes such as a calendar clash, a sense that feedback is ignored or a shift in priorities, each of which needs a different fix.

options.text: Support the product owner's request to the sponsor, since without stakeholder feedback at reviews the team cannot validate the increment against business needs.
options.rationale: The reasoning about feedback is right but compulsion restores attendance, not engagement. The candidate treats a symptom with authority before understanding what produced it.

options.text: Record each review and send the stakeholders a link with a short feedback form, so that they can give their views at a time that suits them each sprint.
options.rationale: This assumes timing is the problem and swaps a conversation for a form. The candidate changes the channel on a guess and loses the interaction the review exists to provide.

questions.explanation: A drop in engagement with a communication event that has not itself changed means something changed for the audience: their workload, their priorities, a clash in the calendar or a belief that their input goes nowhere. Each cause has a different fix, so choosing one before asking is a guess. Compulsion can restore the attendance figure without restoring the feedback the event is there to collect.
questions.mindset: When people stop turning up, find out why before redesigning what they stopped turning up to.

questions.stem: You are managing the build of a council leisure centre. Your schedule risk analysis gives a 50% chance of completing by 3 March and an 80% chance by 14 April. The marketing director has asked you for 'the opening date' so that membership launch materials and opening-day tickets can be printed next week. Missing a published opening date would mean refunds and local press coverage. What should you give her?

options.text: The 3 March date, since it is the most likely finish in the analysis and gives the marketing campaign the longest selling period before the summer season.
options.rationale: The candidate confuses the most likely date with a safe one to publish. A 50% date is missed half the time, and here a miss means refunds and press coverage.

options.text: Both dates with their confidence levels, asking the marketing director to choose which one to print, since the public launch is her commitment to make.
options.rationale: She owns the launch, but she asked for a forecast because she cannot judge schedule risk herself. Handing back two numbers without a recommendation passes on the judgement she came to you for.

options.text: A range of March to April, explaining that the schedule analysis does not support printing a single date until the building envelope is complete in January.
options.rationale: This is honest about uncertainty but ignores a real printing deadline. The candidate withholds a usable forecast when the analysis already supports one at a stated confidence.

options.text: The 14 April date, stating that it carries 80% confidence, and explaining that 3 March is the working target the site team is managing to but is only even odds.
options.rationale: A printed, public date is costly to reverse, so it should be quoted at a high confidence level. Stating the confidence and the earlier target lets her see exactly what she is relying on.

questions.explanation: A forecast used for an external, hard-to-reverse commitment should be given at a confidence level that matches the cost of missing it, with that confidence stated beside the date. The most likely date is the right figure to manage the work against and the wrong one to publish, because it is missed half the time. Quoting the confidence is what tells the person relying on a date what they are actually being given.
questions.mindset: Match the confidence of a date to the cost of missing it, and say which confidence you are quoting.

questions.stem: On your ERP rollout, the six workstream leads each set their own red, amber or green status in the fortnightly report. Twice this year a workstream reported green until the week before a milestone and then went straight to red. Each time, you challenged the lead in the steering meeting about why the problem had not been raised earlier. Which two actions should you take?

options.text: Add to each workstream's status its planned and actual deliverable completion and its forecast date, so that the colour is set against evidence.
options.rationale: A colour chosen by judgement leaves room for optimism. Showing the measures beside it lets anyone see when green and the numbers disagree, well before the milestone.

options.text: Change how you respond to an early amber, treating it in private as a request for help rather than questioning the lead in front of the steering group.
options.rationale: Public challenge after a late red teaches leads that raising problems is costly. Making an early warning the cheaper option for the reporter removes the reason to hold it back.

options.text: Require each lead to sign a declaration that their status is accurate, so that a late change to red can be traced back to the person who reported green.
options.rationale: This adds personal exposure to reporting bad news, which is the pressure already keeping statuses green. The candidate reaches for accountability when the problem is the cost of honesty.

options.text: Move the report to a weekly cycle, so that any deterioration in a workstream reaches the steering group within days rather than within a fortnight.
options.rationale: A subjective colour reported more often stays green just as long. The candidate assumes the delay is in the reporting cycle when it is in the decision to report.

options.text: Ask the PMO to audit one workstream at random each fortnight and compare the reported status with what it finds in the work itself.
options.rationale: Audits find some problems after the fact and signal distrust. The candidate adds inspection on top of the causes instead of removing either of them.

questions.explanation: Status that stays green until it suddenly turns red usually has two causes working together: a colour that is a judgement rather than a measurement, and a reporting climate in which an early warning costs the reporter more than a late one. Anchoring status to evidence removes the room for optimism, and answering early bad news with help removes the reason to delay it. Controls that add scrutiny without touching either cause tend to make the colours greener.
questions.mindset: If bad news arrives late, look at what happens to people who bring it early.

questions.stem: A county council is replacing its housing repairs system using a hybrid approach. Match each communication need to the method that suits it best. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Four heads of service with competing priorities must agree which repair categories go live in the first release.
All 450 repairs staff must know that the old system becomes read-only at 18:00 on 28 November.
Repairs operatives need step-by-step guidance on logging a job, to consult on their tablets whenever they meet an unfamiliar screen.

options.text: Interactive communication, such as a facilitated workshop
options.rationale: Agreement among people who disagree is produced by exchange, not by information. Only a two-way, real-time method lets the four heads of service trade priorities and leave with a decision.

options.text: Push communication, such as a targeted message sent to every member of staff
options.rationale: A fixed date that everyone must know cannot depend on people going to look for it. Sending it to each person, with reminders as the date nears, is what gives it reach.

options.text: Pull communication, such as an online knowledge base that users open when they need it
options.rationale: Guidance needed at unpredictable moments is best held where the user can reach it on demand. Pushing it in advance means it is buried in an inbox when the unfamiliar screen appears.

options.text: Formal reporting, such as a monthly status report to the programme board
options.rationale: Not used. A board report serves governance by informing decision-makers about progress. None of the three needs is a governance audience, and a monthly cycle fits none of them.

questions.explanation: Choose the method by what the communication must achieve. A decision that needs agreement among people who disagree needs interaction, because the exchange is the work. A fact everyone must know by a date needs push, because it cannot depend on people looking for it. Reference material needed at unpredictable moments suits pull, because pushing it early means it is lost by the time it is needed.
questions.mindset: Pick the method for what the message must achieve, not for what is easiest to send.

questions.stem: Your laboratory relocation programme reports to its sponsor monthly. Last month the validation of the cold-storage suite slipped three weeks, the first missed milestone in a year. The sponsor has asked for the full programme report weekly from now on. Producing it takes the PMO about six hours, and the other nine workstreams are on track. What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Agree to the weekly full report, since the sponsor is entitled to set the reporting frequency and has a fresh reason to want closer visibility.
options.rationale: The sponsor does have that right, which makes this defensible. But it answers the request rather than the need, spending six hours a week mostly on nine workstreams nobody is worried about.

options.text: Offer a short weekly update on the cold-storage recovery until it is back on plan, keeping the full programme report on its monthly cycle.
options.rationale: The sponsor's concern is one workstream that has just failed. Closer sight of that recovery meets the need behind the request, costs little and keeps the routine report from filling with on-track detail.

options.text: Give the sponsor live access to the programme plan and dashboard, so that progress on any workstream can be checked at whatever frequency suits them.
options.rationale: Access to data is not assurance about a recovery. The candidate offers more information in general when the sponsor needs an interpreted view of one specific risk.

options.text: Explain the six-hour cost of a weekly report and propose keeping the monthly cycle, with an immediate exception report if any milestone comes under threat.
options.rationale: This is efficient and reasonable in principle, but it treats the request as a cost to be resisted. The sponsor gets nothing more on the one area that has just gone wrong.

questions.explanation: A request for more reporting usually expresses a need for assurance about something specific. Meeting that underlying need, with closer sight of the part that went wrong for as long as it remains at risk, gives the requester more than they asked for at a fraction of the cost and keeps routine reporting from being diluted. Complying literally and declining on cost both respond to the request rather than to the reason for it.
questions.mindset: Answer the worry behind a reporting request, not just the request.

questions.stem: Your bank's lead architect added a line to the quarterly board pack: 'Technical debt in the payments integration layer is significant and growing.' The board noted it without discussion. Your release data show that each change touching that layer now takes three weeks longer than a year ago, and both regulatory changes due next year touch it. What should you do before the next board?

options.text: Invite the lead architect to present a technical briefing on the integration layer, so that board members can understand the scale of the problem first-hand.
options.rationale: More technical depth goes to an audience that could not act on the technical framing the first time. The candidate assumes the board lacked understanding rather than a choice to make.

options.text: Raise the item to red in the board pack's risk summary, attaching the architect's full assessment as an appendix for members who want to read the detail.
options.rationale: A red rating is louder but still not actionable, and an appendix is rarely read. The candidate increases the urgency of the message without changing what it asks of the reader.

options.text: Rewrite the item to set out the effect on the two regulatory deadlines, the options for addressing it with their costs, and the decision the board is asked to take.
options.rationale: The board did not act because nothing told it what the problem would cost or what it could do. Stating consequences, options and the decision needed puts the issue in terms the board owns.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to raise the issue with the board chair privately, since a sponsor-led conversation is more likely to get the item onto the agenda.
options.rationale: Agenda time does not help if the item still arrives as a technical condition. The candidate fixes who carries the message when the problem is how the message is framed.

questions.explanation: A senior audience acts on consequences and choices, not on technical conditions. An issue reported in the language of the people who found it will be noted and left, because the reader cannot tell what it will cost them or what they are being asked to do. Translating it into effects on outcomes the audience owns, the options available and the decision needed is what turns information into something a sponsor or board can act on.
questions.mindset: Report so the reader can decide, not so the writer has said it.

questions.stem: Five agile teams on a ticketing platform hold a cross-team coordination call every working day. It has grown to 16 attendees for 30 minutes. A sprint is 10 working days and the blended staff cost is €70 an hour. The proposal is to limit the call to one representative per team plus the product owner, for 15 minutes daily.

blanks.label: Person-hours spent on the call per sprint today
blanks.rationale: Attendees × duration × occurrences: 16 × 0.5 hours × 10 days = 80 person-hours per sprint.

blanks.label: Person-hours per sprint under the proposal
blanks.rationale: Five representatives plus the product owner is six people: 6 × 0.25 hours × 10 days = 15 person-hours per sprint.

blanks.label: Saving per sprint, in €
blanks.rationale: The reduction is 80 − 15 = 65 person-hours, and 65 × €70 = €4,550 per sprint.

questions.explanation: Communication has a cost that can be planned like any other, and for a recurring meeting it is attendees × duration × frequency. Working it out turns a vague sense that a meeting is too big into a figure that can be weighed against what the meeting achieves. A saving from a smaller meeting is only real if the representatives have a dependable route for carrying information back to their teams, so the plan has to include that route.
questions.mindset: Cost a recurring meeting before deciding it is worth keeping as it is.

questions.stem: A developer who is deaf has joined your distributed product team. The team holds its daily stand-up, refinement and retrospective as video calls, and the developer has said in a message that some of the calls are hard to follow. You want the developer to take full part in all three events. What should you do first?

options.text: Turn on automatic live captions for all team calls and ask everyone to keep their cameras on so that each speaker's face can be clearly seen.
options.rationale: This may well help, but it is a guess about someone else's needs. Automatic captions often struggle with technical vocabulary, and the candidate decides on the developer's behalf.

options.text: Move the stand-up to a written update in the team chat, so that every team member can contribute to it and read it on equal terms each morning.
options.rationale: This changes an event for the whole team on an assumption, and loses the conversation the stand-up exists for. The candidate has not checked whether it is what the developer wants.

options.text: Ask the developer which events are hardest to follow and what would help in each, then agree changes with the team based on that conversation.
options.rationale: The developer knows which barriers matter and what works for them. Starting there avoids choosing an adjustment that misses the real problem or changes events for nobody's benefit.

options.text: Book a sign language interpreter for every video call, arranging the booking through the organisation's workplace adjustments service in advance.
options.rationale: Many deaf people do not use sign language, so this assumes a need that may not exist. Using the adjustments service is right; choosing the adjustment before asking is not.

questions.explanation: Adapting communication for an individual starts with that person's own account of what works, because the same label covers people with very different needs and preferences. A well-meant adjustment chosen on someone's behalf can miss the actual barrier and may change an event for everyone without helping the person it was meant for. Ask, agree, try it, then check again after a sprint or two.
questions.mindset: Ask the person what works before deciding what they need.

questions.stem: Your contractor is replacing a rail bridge, and the traffic management plan makes the project responsible for notifying affected parties of road closures. At 16:00 on Friday the highway authority confirms that Monday's 06:00 closure will now be at Mill Lane junction instead of Station Road. The bus operator, the ambulance service and 300 households were told Station Road. Your communications plan sends changes in the Thursday bulletin. What should you do?

options.text: Ask the highway authority to notify the bus operator and the ambulance service today, since the change was its decision and it holds the emergency-service contacts, and then record the change in Thursday's bulletin.
options.rationale: The authority made the decision, but the traffic management plan places notification with the project, and the 300 households are left to find out from the bulletin after the closure. The candidate routes the message to whoever caused the change rather than to whoever is accountable for communicating it.

options.text: Issue a special edition of the bulletin by email this evening, so that every stakeholder on the list receives an identical message through the agreed channel, and then repeat the change in Thursday's bulletin.
options.rationale: An emailed bulletin on Friday evening gives no confirmation that a bus duty planner or an ambulance control room has seen it before Monday. The candidate keeps the plan's channel when the deadline calls for confirmed receipt by the parties whose operations depend on it.

options.text: Put temporary signs up at both junctions over the weekend and post the change on the project website, so that drivers and residents see the correct information before Monday.
options.rationale: Signs and a web post reach people who happen to pass or to look. The bus operator and the ambulance service must re-plan routes in advance, so the candidate has chosen broadcast channels for parties who need direct notice.

options.text: Phone the bus operator and the ambulance service today, deliver a letter to the affected households over the weekend, and then record the change in Thursday's bulletin.
options.rationale: The weekly cycle was designed for routine change, not for a change that takes effect before the next bulletin. Information arriving after 06:00 on Monday is useless, so the channel has to fit the deadline, while the bulletin still records it.

questions.explanation: A communications plan sets default channels and frequencies for routine information. A change that takes effect before the next scheduled message needs a channel chosen for its deadline and for who must act on it: parties whose operations depend on the information need direct notice they can confirm, while the routine channel still records the change for everyone else. Accountability for notifying follows the plan, not whoever made the decision.
questions.mindset: Let the deadline of the information choose the channel, not the calendar of the plan.

questions.stem: You manage the £48 million build of a new wing for a hospital trust. At 14:00 a local journalist phones you directly. She has a copy of last week's internal status report, which shows the schedule as red, and wants a comment by 17:00. The trust's policy is that all media enquiries are handled by its communications office. Your sponsor is on leave this week. What should you do?

options.text: Give the journalist a brief factual statement that the red status reflects one delayed package with a recovery plan in place, so that the leaked report is not published without context.
options.rationale: Context would help, and the facts are yours, which is what makes this tempting. But the candidate speaks to the press for the trust against its policy, and an unplanned quote from the project manager can become the story.

options.text: Find out how the report reached the journalist before responding, so that the trust can judge how much else has been disclosed and what any response will need to cover.
options.rationale: The leak matters, but tracing it is not on the critical path for a 17:00 deadline and is not the project manager's investigation to run. The candidate diagnoses first when the immediate need is to get the enquiry to its owner.

options.text: Phone the sponsor on leave to agree what should be said to the journalist, since a public comment on the project's status needs the authority of the person accountable for it.
options.rationale: The sponsor is accountable for the project, not for the trust's media handling. The candidate escalates up the project line when the policy already names a different owner who is at work today.

options.text: Tell the journalist that the trust's communications office will answer her enquiry, then brief that office straight away on what the report shows and the recovery plan behind it.
options.rationale: The policy names the owner of media responses, and the owner can only answer well with the facts. Passing the enquiry on and briefing the office within the hour meets the 17:00 deadline without the project speaking for the trust.

questions.explanation: When an organisation names an owner for a type of communication, such as media enquiries, the project manager's job is to route the request to that owner quickly and equip them with the facts, not to answer on the organisation's behalf or wait for the project's own hierarchy. Holding accurate information does not confer the authority to release it externally; the useful contribution is making sure the owner speaks from the facts.
questions.mindset: Get the message to its owner fast, with the facts attached.

questions.stem: Halfway through a nuclear decommissioning project, the site's security team issues a new rule: technical documents may no longer be exchanged with suppliers by email and must go through the site's secure document portal. Your overseas design supplier says the portal is slower and that queries now take days to resolve instead of hours. The rule applies to every project on the site. Which two actions should you take?

options.text: Update the communications management plan to make the portal the channel for documents, and agree with the supplier a twice-weekly call for resolving queries about portal items.
options.rationale: The rule changes the channel for documents, not the need for quick resolution. Separating the exchange of documents from the conversation about them keeps the record secure while restoring a fast route for clarifying queries.

options.text: Arrange a joint session with the security team and the supplier to set up the supplier's portal access, folder structure and alerts so the portal works day to day.
options.rationale: Much of the slowness of a new channel is set-up: missing alerts, unclear folders, accounts that do not work. Fixing these with the people who own the portal makes the mandated channel usable rather than working round it.

options.text: Apply to the security team for an exemption for this supplier, setting out the schedule impact of slower query resolution and the supplier's existing security credentials.
options.rationale: An exemption request is legitimate in form, but the rule is site-wide and nothing has yet been done to make the portal workable. The candidate spends effort escaping a constraint before trying to adapt to it.

options.text: Keep using email for routine queries that contain no drawings or specifications, and use the portal only for the documents themselves, so that daily traffic is not slowed down.
options.rationale: Queries about technical documents usually quote them, and the rule covers technical content. The candidate draws a line the security team did not draw and creates a disclosure risk in order to recover speed.

options.text: Record the slower query turnaround as a risk to the design schedule and report it to the sponsor, asking whether the project should seek a change to the site rule.
options.rationale: Recording the impact is reasonable, but asking the sponsor to challenge a site-wide security rule treats a fixed constraint as negotiable. The candidate escalates before changing how the project communicates within it.

questions.explanation: When an organisational rule changes how a project may communicate, the work is to redesign communication inside the constraint: update the plan, make the mandated channel usable, and separate what the rule controls from what it does not. Seeking exemptions or escalating treats a constraint as a problem to escape, and quietly drawing new boundaries around a security rule creates exactly the exposure the rule was written to prevent.
questions.mindset: When the channel is fixed for you, make it work before trying to get out of it.

questions.stem: On a ferry terminal upgrade, three messages failed to have their intended effect. Match each to the point in the sender-receiver model where it broke down. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: The structural engineer sent the port's operations director a fortnightly update made up entirely of load calculations and design-code references, although the director had told him he could not use them.
The site supervisor briefed thirty operatives on a changed crane exclusion zone while standing beside a running piling rig, and several later said they had caught only part of it.
The project manager emailed the steel supplier a revised delivery window, saw the read receipt and treated it as agreed; the supplier delivered on the original date.

options.text: Encoding: the sender put the message in a form the receiver could not use
options.rationale: The content may have been accurate, but the sender chose a form the receiver had already said he could not work with. The failure sits in the sender's choice of form, before the message was ever sent.

options.text: Noise: something in the environment interfered with the message in transit
options.rationale: The message and the audience were right, but the setting degraded what reached them. Noise is dealt with by changing the conditions, such as moving the briefing away from the rig, and by checking understanding afterwards.

options.text: Feedback: the sender took receipt as agreement without confirming the response
options.rationale: A read receipt shows that a message arrived, not that it was understood or accepted. The sender closed the loop on an assumption, and only an explicit reply would have shown that the supplier had not agreed.

options.text: Decoding: the receiver read the words correctly but attached a different meaning to them
options.rationale: Not used. Decoding fails when a receiver confidently takes a different meaning from a clear message. In each case here the problem arose elsewhere: an unusable form, a noisy setting, or an unconfirmed response.

questions.explanation: Locating where a communication failed tells you which fix will work. A poor choice of form by the sender is fixed by tailoring the message to the receiver; noise is fixed by changing the conditions of transmission; a missing response is fixed by asking for a reply that shows understanding or agreement. Treating every failure as a need to send the message again simply repeats the same breakdown.
questions.mindset: Find where a message broke before deciding how to send it again.

questions.stem: An agile team at an online fashion retailer releases a redesigned returns process next week. The product owner is writing a release note for each affected audience. Complete each sentence with the content that should lead. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: For the customer service team, who will take calls from customers using the new process, the note should lead with
For the finance director, who signs off refund liabilities at each month end, the note should lead with
For the warehouse returns team, who unpack and process the parcels that come back, the note should lead with

options.text: what customers will see at each step and how to answer the questions it is likely to raise
options.rationale: Customer service staff act on what customers experience and ask about. Leading with that equips them for the calls they will take in the first week, which is when a new process generates the most questions.

options.text: the expected change in refund timing and its effect on month-end liabilities
options.rationale: The finance director owns the liability figures, so the release matters to her through its effect on them. Leading with timing and money puts the change in the terms she signs off.

options.text: the change to returns labels and the date parcels carrying the new labels will start arriving
options.rationale: The warehouse handles physical parcels, so what changes for them is what arrives and when. Giving the label change and its start date lets them prepare before the first new parcel lands.

options.text: the user stories completed in the sprint and the acceptance criteria each one met
options.rationale: Not used. Stories and acceptance criteria are the delivery team's view of the work. None of the three audiences acts on them, and leading with them leaves each reader to work out what the change means for them.

questions.explanation: The same change needs a different lead message for each audience, chosen by what that audience must do differently as a result. Operational teams need what they will encounter and when; financial decision-makers need the effect on the figures they own. Leading with the delivery team's view of the work, such as stories and acceptance criteria, describes what was built rather than what it means for the reader.
questions.mindset: Lead with what the reader will do differently, not with what the team did.

questions.stem: On a hotel refurbishment, a ductwork subcontractor installed to a superseded drawing on Thursday, although the revised drawing was issued on Tuesday. The diagram shows each handover in the drawing-revision path and how it currently works. Select the handover whose design allowed the revision to be missed.

graphic.title: Five handovers in the drawing-revision path, from architect to subcontractors
graphic.caption: Select a handover. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between them, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Architect to design manager: revision request logged in the change register the same day
regions.rationale: The request was logged promptly and the revision was produced by Tuesday. Blaming the start of the path assumes the problem was late design, which the dates in the stem rule out.

regions.label: Design manager to document control: revised drawing issued with a transmittal and a new revision letter
regions.rationale: A transmittal and a new revision letter are what make a revision traceable. This handover worked, and choosing it confuses a well-controlled issue with a delivered one.

regions.label: Document control to site portal: superseded drawing marked void and replaced within two hours
regions.rationale: The portal held the right drawing from Tuesday. The candidate assumes the record was wrong, when the record was correct and nobody downstream was working from it.

regions.label: Site portal to site manager: automatic email alert sent on every new revision
regions.rationale: The alert put the revision in front of the site manager on Tuesday. Choosing it stops tracing at the first person told, rather than following the message to the people who acted on it.

regions.label: Site manager to subcontractors: drawing packs printed each Monday for the week's work briefings
regions.rationale: A weekly print cycle cannot carry a revision issued on Tuesday, so the subcontractor worked all week from Monday's pack. Every handover before this one was effectively real time; this one silently reintroduced a week's delay.

questions.explanation: When a message fails to reach the people who act on it, trace the path handover by handover and look for the step whose cycle or medium cannot carry a change that arrives between cycles. A batched or weekly channel downstream of real-time ones quietly reintroduces the delay the earlier steps removed, so the end of a communication path needs as much design as its start.
questions.mindset: Follow a message to the person who acts on it, not just to the first person who receives it.

questions.stem: Your team is building a claims portal for an insurance client under a time-and-materials contract. At the client's request, the product owner has sent the team's velocity chart every fortnight. Velocity fell from 34 points to 27 last sprint after the team took on a complex integration, and the client's programme director has asked for a written explanation and a plan to restore it to 34. What should you do?

options.text: Meet the programme director to find out what decision the velocity chart is informing, and offer a release burn-up with a forecast date range that answers that question directly.
options.rationale: Velocity is a team planning measure, and reading it as output invites exactly this demand. Finding what the director needs to know, usually when the scope will be done, and reporting that directly removes the misreading at source.

options.text: Send the written explanation the director asked for, setting out the integration's complexity and showing that velocity is expected to recover once the integration work is complete.
options.rationale: This is honest and responsive, which is why it is attractive. But it accepts the premise that velocity is a performance target to be defended, so the same request will come back the next time the number dips.

options.text: Run a short session for the client's programme team explaining how story points and velocity work, so that future movements in the chart are read with the right expectations.
options.rationale: Education helps, but it keeps a team-internal measure as the client's main view and relies on every future reader remembering the session. The candidate fixes the reader rather than asking whether this is the right thing to report.

options.text: Agree with the team to re-estimate the remaining backlog with the integration's complexity included, so that velocity stays steadier and the reported figure is more consistent.
options.rationale: Re-estimating to steady the number lets an external audience shape internal estimation, which is how story points inflate. The candidate improves the metric's appearance instead of questioning its use.

questions.explanation: When a stakeholder reacts to a metric as though it measured something it does not, the problem is the choice of measure, not the reading of it. Team-internal planning measures such as velocity become targets once they are reported outward, and targets distort estimation. Start from the decision the stakeholder is trying to make and report the measure that informs it, such as forecast completion against scope.
questions.mindset: Before defending a number, ask whether it is the right number to be reporting.

questions.stem: Your steering group meets in 30 minutes to make the go-live decision for a new warehouse management system. The pack you circulated yesterday reports all testing complete. Ten minutes ago the test lead told you that this morning's peak-volume rerun showed pick confirmations taking 9 seconds against a 2-second target. The cause is not yet known and could lie in the test environment. What should you do?

options.text: Open the meeting by telling the group about the test result, what is and is not yet known about its cause, and when the investigation will report, before the go-live item is discussed.
options.rationale: The group is about to decide on information that is now incomplete. Telling them at once, with the uncertainty stated, lets the people with the authority decide whether to proceed, defer or make the decision conditional.

options.text: Ask the chair to move the go-live decision to a later meeting, explaining that a new test result needs investigating before the group can decide on a sound and complete basis.
options.rationale: This protects the decision from bad information, and it may be where the group ends up. But it decides for them that deferral is the answer and withholds facts they could use to choose a conditional go-live instead.

options.text: Phone the sponsor before the meeting to brief her on the test result, and agree with her how and when it should be presented to the steering group so that she is not caught unprepared.
options.rationale: Avoiding surprises for the sponsor is a sound instinct. But the decision belongs to the group, and making disclosure depend on a private agreement about timing risks the group deciding without facts it needs.

options.text: Amend your recommendation in the pack to no-go and present the test result as the reason, so that the group does not commit to a launch that may fail under peak-volume conditions.
options.rationale: The result may yet be an environment fault, so a firm no-go overstates what is known. The candidate swaps one unfounded certainty for another instead of presenting the uncertainty as it stands.

questions.explanation: When new information materially changes the basis for a decision about to be taken, it goes to the decision-makers before the decision, stated with its uncertainty, even if it is incomplete. Holding it until it is confirmed, filtering it through one person, or converting it into a recommendation it does not yet support each lets the decision be made on a picture the project manager knows to be out of date.
questions.mindset: Information that changes a decision belongs in the room before the decision, uncertainty and all.

questions.stem: Your infusion pump project has a hardware workstream run to a stage-gated plan and a firmware workstream run in sprints. In the monthly report, hardware calls a component 'complete' when its design is frozen; firmware calls a feature 'complete' when it meets the sprint's definition of done, before system verification. The quality director has twice assumed 'complete' meant verified. What should you do?

options.text: Ask the sponsor to direct both workstreams to use the stage-gated definition of complete, so that the report follows the organisation's governance framework rather than team conventions.
options.rationale: This escalates something the project manager can settle, and imposing design-freeze language on firmware loses what sprint-level done tells the reader. The candidate seeks authority that is not needed.

options.text: Add a footnote to each workstream's section of the report explaining what that workstream means by complete, so that every reader can interpret the two sections correctly.
options.rationale: Footnotes keep two meanings for one word in the same report and rely on readers reading them, which the quality director has already shown is unreliable. The candidate documents the ambiguity rather than removing it.

options.text: Agree with both workstream leads a single set of status terms with written definitions, add them to the communications plan and the report key, and use them from the next report.
options.rationale: Defining the report's own vocabulary is within the project manager's remit and needs nobody else's approval. A shared, published definition removes the ambiguity for every reader, not only for the one who raised it.

options.text: Brief the quality director in person on how each workstream uses the term, and offer the same briefing to any other report reader who raises the same misunderstanding.
options.rationale: This fixes one reader's understanding and waits for others to be misled first. The candidate treats a defect in the report as a gap in one person's knowledge.

questions.explanation: When the same word carries different meanings in one report, readers apply whichever meaning they already hold, and the cost falls on the decisions taken from it. In a hybrid environment the project manager owns the shared vocabulary of integrated reporting and can define it directly. Defining terms once for every reader removes the ambiguity at source, which annotations and individual briefings do not.
questions.mindset: If one word means two things in your report, fix the word, not the reader.

questions.stem: Your agile team is building a student enrolment app for a university. Admissions and finance staff have started sending requests straight to individual developers through chat. Some small requests are done within a day, others disappear, and the product owner often learns of a change only at the sprint review. Two heads of department now complain that their requests are being ignored. Which two actions should you take?

options.text: Agree with the team and the product owner that requests arriving by chat are passed to the product owner, and tell requesters that this is the route from now on.
options.rationale: The product owner owns what the team works on, so requests that bypass her are decisions taken by whoever happens to be asked. One known route puts each request in front of the person who can weigh it against everything else.

options.text: Give the admissions and finance staff read access to the backlog, with a view showing each of their requests and its current status and priority.
options.rationale: The complaint is that requests vanish. Letting requesters see where their item stands turns silence into an answer, even when the answer is that it is not yet prioritised.

options.text: Allow developers to complete chat requests estimated at under two hours directly, and send everything larger to the product owner for prioritisation.
options.rationale: A size threshold feels pragmatic, but small requests still change the product without the product owner's knowledge and still compete for capacity. The candidate keeps a second, invisible intake route open.

options.text: Ask the heads of admissions and finance to stop their staff contacting developers directly, and to send all requests through a monthly request form instead.
options.rationale: Closing the side channel is right in spirit, but a monthly form slows legitimate requests and sends them to nobody in particular. The candidate fixes the channel without connecting it to the person who decides.

options.text: Have the scrum master collect chat requests from the developers each day and log them in a shared spreadsheet that is reviewed at sprint planning.
options.rationale: This captures requests but creates a parallel list outside the backlog, owned by someone who does not prioritise. The candidate improves record-keeping while leaving the decision with the wrong person.

questions.explanation: Requests about what a team should build need one route to the person accountable for prioritising them, and requesters need to see what has happened to what they asked for. Side channels to individual team members make prioritisation decisions invisibly, and logging or filtering them without passing them to the owner keeps the decision in the wrong place. Visibility of status answers most complaints about being ignored.
questions.mindset: Send each request to the person who decides on it, and let the requester see what happened next.

questions.stem: You are managing the supply of a bottling line to a drinks manufacturer. On a phone call this morning, the client's project director agreed to your request to move the factory acceptance test from 12 May to 19 May. The contract states that test dates may be changed only by written notice between the two named contract representatives, who are you and the director. What should you do?

options.text: Send the director a written notice confirming the new test date of 19 May, as the contract requires, and copy the people on both sides who need to plan around it.
options.rationale: The phone call created an agreement in principle, but the contract says the change only takes effect in writing. Sending the notice promptly, while both sides remember the call the same way, completes the communication in the form that counts.

options.text: Record the agreement in your call notes and the project log, and rely on the director's word, since he is the client's named representative and senior enough to decide.
options.rationale: The candidate treats the director's authority as enough on its own. His authority is not in doubt; the form is, and a private note of a phone call does not meet a clause that asks for written notice between the parties.

options.text: Report the new test date in your next monthly progress report to the client, which reaches the director and his team and puts the change on the formal project record.
options.rationale: A progress report is not the notice the contract specifies, and it may arrive weeks after people have started planning for 12 May. The candidate confuses putting something on record with communicating it in the prescribed way.

options.text: Ask the director to send you written confirmation of the new date when he has time, so that the formal record of the change comes from the client who agreed to it.
options.rationale: Either representative can give notice, and you asked for the change. Leaving the paperwork to a busy counterpart makes the record depend on someone else's priorities and leaves the date legally unchanged in the meantime.

questions.explanation: When a contract prescribes how a decision must be communicated, a spoken agreement is only the first step; the communication is not complete until it takes the form the contract names. The party who needs the change has the strongest reason to formalise it, and the sooner it is written the less room there is for the two sides to remember the conversation differently.
questions.mindset: An agreement the contract says must be written down does not exist until it is.

questions.stem: The head of engineering, who line-manages most of your agile team, has asked you to forward him the full notes from each retrospective so that he can 'keep a finger on the pulse'. The team writes candidly in retrospectives, including about friction with other departments and about one another's working habits. The team has never discussed who sees the notes. What should you do?

options.text: Forward the full notes as he has asked, since he line-manages the team and openness with management is part of how an agile team earns trust from the wider organisation.
options.rationale: The candidate equates transparency about work with exposing a candid discussion. Once the team learns its line manager reads every word, people will say less, and the retrospective stops surfacing the problems it exists to find.

options.text: Decline the request politely, telling him that retrospectives are confidential to the team and that nothing discussed in them can be shared with anyone outside it.
options.rationale: This protects the team but treats confidentiality as absolute and leaves a reasonable need unmet. He will look for the information elsewhere, and the team may well have been happy to share its actions.

options.text: Write him your own summary after each retrospective with names and personal remarks removed, so that he gets the substance of the discussion without individuals being exposed.
options.rationale: Anonymising feels safe, but you are deciding on the team's behalf what leaves the room. In a small team remarks are often traceable, and knowing a summary goes upward still changes what people are willing to say.

options.text: Ask the team what they are comfortable sharing, then offer him the improvement actions and themes they agree to publish, explaining why the discussion itself stays in the room.
options.rationale: His interest in how the team is doing is legitimate and can be met with outcomes. Letting the team set the boundary, and telling him openly where it is, protects candour without shutting a senior stakeholder out.

questions.explanation: Candour in a retrospective depends on participants knowing in advance who will read what they say. Requests for visibility from outside the team are usually legitimate and can be met with what the team decides to do, rather than the raw discussion that led there. The boundary belongs to the team, should be agreed before it is tested, and should be stated plainly to whoever asks.
questions.mindset: Share what a team learns, and let the team decide how much of how it learned it leaves the room.

questions.stem: Your agile team's chat workspace receives about 250 automated messages a day from the build server, the issue tracker and the monitoring tool, all in one shared channel. Last week a production alert about a failing payment job sat unread for five hours, and two developers have muted the channel entirely. A developer proposes switching off all issue tracker notifications to cut the volume. What should you do first?

options.text: Review with the team which message types led anyone to act over the last two sprints, and use that to decide what stays in the shared channel and what goes elsewhere.
options.rationale: Routing can only be designed once you know which messages prompt action and for whom. Two sprints of history give that evidence quickly and let the team agree a design rather than argue about volume.

options.text: Switch off the issue tracker notifications as proposed, since they make up the largest share of the volume and the team can check the tracker directly whenever it needs to.
options.rationale: The candidate cuts by source and volume rather than by usefulness. Some tracker messages, such as an item assigned to you or newly blocked, may be the ones people act on, while the noise that buried the alert stays.

options.text: Move production monitoring alerts into a separate channel with sound notifications turned on for everyone, and leave the build and tracker messages where they are for now.
options.rationale: This may be part of the eventual design, but it fixes one symptom before anyone knows which messages matter to whom. Alerting everyone audibly also spreads responsibility so thinly that nobody in particular owns the response.

options.text: Agree a working rule that everyone checks the shared channel at least hourly, and ask the two developers to unmute it so that urgent alerts are seen and handled promptly.
options.rationale: The candidate asks people to absorb the noise instead of reducing it. Muting is the evidence that the channel's signal has been lost, and an hourly check would still have left the payment alert waiting.

questions.explanation: When a channel carries more than people can read, they filter it themselves, usually by ignoring it, and the important message is lost along with the noise. Redesign starts from which messages lead to action and by whom: those needing immediate action by a named person go to an interruptive route, and the rest to a digest or a place people pull from. Cutting by source or by volume without that evidence risks removing the signal.
questions.mindset: Design a channel around the messages people act on, not the messages systems can send.

questions.stem: Your firm is delivering a €6 million building management system upgrade under a contract that requires a formal monthly progress report, signed by you, to the client's contract manager. The client's day-to-day project lead says nobody reads the reports and asks you to stop producing them and hold a weekly call instead. She is not the contract manager. A weekly call would genuinely help. What should you do?

options.text: Agree to replace the report with the weekly call, and confirm the new arrangement by email to the project lead so that there is a written record of what the client asked for.
options.rationale: The candidate treats a written request as a contract change. The project lead has no authority to vary the contract, so the obligation stands, and in any later dispute the missing reports count against your firm.

options.text: Start the weekly call, keep issuing the monthly report until the client's contract manager agrees in writing to change the requirement, and raise that change with him.
options.rationale: This adds the channel that helps straight away and routes the removal of the contracted one to the person who can authorise it. The report continues only until the change is agreed, so no obligation lapses in the meantime.

options.text: Keep producing the monthly report as the contract requires and decline the weekly call, explaining to the project lead that the reporting arrangements are set out in the contract.
options.rationale: The contract sets a minimum, not a maximum. Refusing a useful extra channel because the contract does not mention it confuses compliance with communication and damages a working relationship for nothing.

options.text: Start the weekly call straight away, and ask the project lead to raise the change with her contract manager, pausing the monthly report while she does so on your behalf.
options.rationale: The route to the contract manager is right but the timing is wrong. Pausing a contractual deliverable before the change is agreed is a breach, however likely the agreement looks.

questions.explanation: A reporting requirement written into a contract can be changed only by the people with authority to vary the contract, however reasonable the request and however closely the requester works with you day to day. Extra, informal channels can be added freely because the contract sets a floor; removing a contracted one has to wait for the formal change, and the existing obligation runs until then.
questions.mindset: Add communication freely, but remove a contracted channel only through the contract.

questions.stem: Your hybrid programme depends on an overseas engineering supplier delivering a control module by 30 June. In this morning's video call with eight people, you asked the supplier's team lead to confirm the date. After a pause she said, 'We will do our very best; it may be a little difficult.' Your steering report is due tomorrow and has a column for supplier dates confirmed. What should you do?

options.text: Record 30 June as confirmed in the steering report, since she did not reject the date, and track the module closely through the supplier's weekly progress updates from now on.
options.rationale: The candidate treats the absence of a refusal as agreement. Her wording carries a clear reservation, and reporting it as a confirmation passes a commitment to the steering group that was never actually given.

options.text: Record 30 June as at risk in the steering report, quoting her words, so that the steering group can see the supplier has not yet given a firm commitment to the date.
options.rationale: This is more honest, but it reports your reading of a hedge without testing it. Quoting her in a governance document can embarrass the supplier, and the steering group still lacks the date the supplier could actually meet.

options.text: Speak to the team lead one to one today, asking what would make 30 June achievable and what date she would be confident in, before you complete the supplier column.
options.rationale: A private conversation removes the audience that may have made a direct answer hard. Asking what is needed, rather than whether the date is fine, gives you a real position to report tomorrow.

options.text: Email the supplier's account director asking for written confirmation of the 30 June date, so that the commitment is formal and comes from someone with authority over the team.
options.rationale: The candidate escalates before understanding the problem. A senior signature on a date the team doubts recreates the same uncertainty with more at stake, and going over her head makes candour less likely next time.

questions.explanation: Hesitation, qualified language and silence in a group setting can signal a concern the speaker is not comfortable stating openly, particularly to a client in front of others. Before reporting a commitment, test what was meant in a setting where candour is easier, and ask what would be needed rather than whether everything is fine. What gets reported should be the speaker's actual position, not the listener's interpretation of their words.
questions.mindset: Find out what an answer means before reporting what it said.

questions.stem: On your hybrid fibre-network rollout, the heads of field operations and of customer service disagree about when customers should be told their installation dates. Over three days their email thread has grown to 31 messages with 22 people copied in, and the tone has sharpened with each reply. They report to different directors. The decision on notification timing is within your delegated authority. What should you do?

options.text: Reply to all with a neutral summary of both positions and your decision on notification timing, so that everyone copied in has the same record of how the matter was settled.
options.rationale: This uses your authority but settles the matter in the medium that inflamed it. Announcing a winner in front of 22 people, without either head being heard in a conversation, risks hardening the disagreement rather than ending it.

options.text: Ask both heads to stop the thread and set out their positions in a short paper each, and then decide the timing yourself once you have read and compared the two papers.
options.rationale: The candidate moves from one lean, written medium to another. Papers keep two people arguing at a distance, add days, and do nothing about the friction that the thread has built up between them.

options.text: Bring the two heads together on a call this week to work through the timing, make the decision, and then send one short summary of it to the people on the thread.
options.rationale: A live conversation with only the two owners lets each be heard and lets you probe the reasoning. The written summary afterwards closes the thread for everyone copied in, using writing for the record rather than the argument.

options.text: Escalate the disagreement to the two directors and ask them to agree a position between them, since the heads report through different lines and the thread is now widely visible.
options.rationale: The decision is within your delegated authority. Escalating because of tone and visibility hands away a decision you own and draws two directors into something that does not need them.

questions.explanation: Lean, written channels suit simple and uncontentious information. As disagreement and emotion rise, they amplify misreading, and a long copy list turns positions into public stances that are harder to step back from. Contested matters belong in a richer, synchronous medium with only the people who own them, after which writing does what it does best: recording the outcome for everyone who needs to know.
questions.mindset: Match the medium to the heat of the message, then write down the result.

questions.stem: You are managing the relocation of a 1,800-person tax agency office to a new building. The communications plan relies on a monthly newsletter emailed to all staff. A pulse survey shows that 70% of staff get most of their information about the move from their line manager, and only 12% have read a newsletter. Several team leaders admit they know little more than their staff. What should you do?

options.text: Redesign the newsletter with a shorter format, clearer headlines and a summary of key dates, and send it fortnightly instead of monthly to raise readership among staff.
options.rationale: The candidate polishes a channel the evidence says staff do not use. Doubling its frequency doubles the cost, and it ignores where staff actually turn for answers about the move.

options.text: Ask the agency's directors to send an all-staff email telling everyone to read the newsletter, stressing that it is the official source of information on the move from now on.
options.rationale: This tries to change the audience's behaviour to fit the plan. Instructions to read rarely change reading habits, and team leaders would still be fielding questions they cannot answer.

options.text: Revise the plan so that team leaders receive a short briefing pack before each newsletter goes out, and use them as the main channel to staff, keeping the newsletter as a reference.
options.rationale: Staff already go to their line managers, so equipping those managers puts accurate information where people look for it. The newsletter remains useful as the written reference the briefings can point to.

options.text: Hold a series of open town-hall sessions for all staff in the new building, where you present the move plan in person and answer questions directly from the floor.
options.rationale: Town halls are rich and visible but occasional. They do not reach staff when questions actually arise, and they bypass the line managers whom staff will keep asking between sessions.

questions.explanation: A communications plan is a working assumption about how information will reach people, and evidence about where they actually get it should change the plan. When an audience relies on an intermediary, equipping that intermediary is usually more effective than trying to pull people towards a channel they have already ignored.
questions.mindset: Send the message through the route people already trust, and make sure that route knows the answer.

questions.stem: Your agile team builds the customer app for an energy retailer. The PMO requires every project to submit a monthly report in its standard template, which includes a milestone table with planned and forecast dates. The team says the template 'does not fit agile' and wants to send a link to its online board instead. The PMO uses the template to compile a portfolio view for the executive committee. What should you do?

options.text: Send the PMO the link to the board with a covering note on how to read it, and offer a walk-through so that the PMO can extract what it needs for the portfolio view.
options.rationale: The candidate shifts the translation work onto the PMO, which has to produce a comparable view across every project. A team board answers the team's questions, not the executive committee's.

options.text: Complete the template with a full task-level milestone schedule for the next six months, so that the PMO receives the same level of detail it gets from predictive projects.
options.rationale: This manufactures precision the approach does not hold. Dates set at task level six months out will move every sprint, and each revision erodes the PMO's trust in what the team reports.

options.text: Ask the PMO to create a separate agile reporting template for the team, with velocity, burn-up and backlog measures in place of the milestone table, before the next submission.
options.rationale: The candidate asks a portfolio function to redesign its reporting for one team. A bespoke template breaks the comparability the executive committee relies on, and the next report is held up while it is built.

options.text: Complete the template each month, filling the milestone table with the planned releases and forecast date ranges taken from the backlog and the team's own delivery data.
options.rationale: The PMO's need is a comparable portfolio view, and release-level milestones with honest ranges meet it from data the team already has. The format is respected without inventing detail to fill it.

questions.explanation: A governance body's template exists to serve its audience, often by making different projects comparable. An agile team can usually meet that need by translating its own data into the required format at the level it can honestly support, such as releases with forecast ranges, rather than refusing the format or inventing detail to fill it.
questions.mindset: Translate your data into the reader's format rather than asking the reader to learn yours.

questions.stem: The sponsor of a charity's donation platform has started attending your agile team's daily stand-up. She asks each developer for progress updates and has twice reassigned work on the spot. Over two weeks the stand-ups have doubled in length, and developers have stopped mentioning blockers; one told you privately that it feels like an inspection. The sponsor says she attends because she wants to know how things are going. What should you do?

options.text: Meet the sponsor privately, describe the change you have seen in the stand-ups since she began attending, and agree with her a separate way to get the progress information she wants.
options.rationale: She can see only that she is getting information, not what her presence costs. Showing her the effect, and offering a better route to what she needs, protects the event and keeps a supportive sponsor on side.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to stop attending the stand-up, explaining that the event belongs to the developers and that stakeholders should get their information at the sprint review.
options.rationale: The candidate is right about the event's purpose, but the request is blunt and leaves her real need unmet until the next review. She will look for progress information elsewhere, and the relationship pays for it.

options.text: Let the sponsor keep attending but agree with her that she will observe silently and bring any questions or changes to the work to you after the stand-up has finished.
options.rationale: A plausible compromise, but a silent senior observer still changes what people say in front of her. Blockers stay hidden, and her need for information is met only by watching an event not designed for it.

options.text: Raise the effect of the sponsor's attendance at the next retrospective, so that the team can discuss it openly and agree how it wants to handle stakeholders attending stand-ups.
options.rationale: The team may want to discuss it, but the cause lies with someone outside the team and lost blockers are costing time now. It also leaves developers to confront a sponsor on their own behalf.

questions.explanation: When a stakeholder's presence changes a team's communication event, the effect is usually invisible to that stakeholder, who sees only that they are getting information. Showing them the effect privately, and meeting their underlying need by another route, protects the event without turning someone whose support the project needs into an adversary.
questions.mindset: When a stakeholder disrupts a channel, meet the need that brought them there through a better one.

questions.stem: Your hybrid programme relies on a specialist analytics supplier. Over dinner, a contact at another firm tells you in confidence that the supplier is in late-stage talks to be acquired by a competitor of your organisation, which could end your access to the platform. Nothing is public. Your risk register is shared with all 14 workstream leads, two of whom work for the supplier. What should you do?

options.text: Add the risk to the shared register in general terms, describing it as a possible change of ownership at a key supplier, so that it is visible and managed like any other risk.
options.rationale: The instinct for visibility is sound, but even general wording in a register read by the supplier's own leads reveals what you know. It can compromise your source and the supplier's confidential negotiations at once.

options.text: Raise the question directly with the supplier's account director, asking whether any change of ownership is expected that could affect your continued access to the platform.
options.rationale: Asking directly may produce facts, but it signals that you hold confidential information and may expose your source. The supplier may be bound not to answer, and you act before your own organisation has decided its position.

options.text: Take no action on the information until it is confirmed publicly, since it was given in confidence and acting on an unverified report could damage the relationship with the supplier.
options.rationale: This respects the confidence but leaves a potentially serious risk unmanaged. Quiet contingency planning, such as checking data export rights, harms nobody, and waiting for an announcement gives up weeks of options.

options.text: Brief your sponsor privately on the possibility without naming your source, and agree with her how to record and respond to the risk without disclosing it to the supplier's staff.
options.rationale: The risk is real enough to manage and too sensitive for the normal channel. Taking it to the person with authority to decide how it is handled lets contingency work start through restricted routes without breaching the confidence.

questions.explanation: Transparency about risk does not mean every audience sees every risk in the same form. Sensitive information goes first to the person with authority to decide how it is handled, and the response can then be planned through restricted channels, protecting the organisation without breaching a confidence or alerting a party with an interest in the outcome. Deciding who needs to know is part of communicating a risk, not an exception to it.
questions.mindset: Decide who needs to know before deciding how widely to tell.

questions.stem: You manage the £120 million build of a desalination plant for a joint venture between a water utility and an energy company. Each partner has its own sponsor, and each has asked for a monthly report in its own corporate format: the utility emphasises water-quality milestones, the energy company cost and power consumption. Producing both takes four days a month, and last month the two reports gave different forecast completion dates. What should you do?

options.text: Keep both formats but produce them from one master dataset and reconcile the forecast dates before release, so that each sponsor gets its preferred report and the figures match.
options.rationale: This fixes the inconsistency and is a real improvement, but it accepts the premise that two reports are needed. The four days of effort remain, and two narratives with different emphasis still invite the partners to read the project differently.

options.text: Propose to both sponsors a single joint report built from one set of project data, with a section for each partner's priority measures, and ask them to agree it at the next joint board.
options.rationale: Both partners see the same figures and the same forecast, while each can find the measures it cares about. Putting it to the joint board makes the format a shared decision rather than a concession by either side.

options.text: Ask the joint venture's board to choose one partner's corporate format as the project standard, and send that single report to both sponsors from next month onwards.
options.rationale: One report removes the divergence, but adopting one partner's format signals whose priorities count. The other sponsor's measures are pushed to the margins, and the candidate trades inconsistency for a perception of bias.

options.text: Explain the different forecast dates to both sponsors in writing, and add a reconciliation step to your monthly reporting process that checks the two reports against each other.
options.rationale: The candidate corrects this month's error and adds a control, but leaves the duplication that caused it. A reconciliation step catches divergence after the fact instead of removing the conditions that produce it.

questions.explanation: When several sponsors ask for separate reports, the risk is not only effort but divergent versions of the truth that can set partners against each other. One report from one dataset, arranged so each party's priorities are visible, gives everyone the same picture. A request for separate formats is a preference to be negotiated with the people who made it, not a requirement to be accepted as given.
questions.mindset: Give everyone the same truth, arranged so each can find what they care about.

questions.stem: On a new university science building, this afternoon's change control board rejected the chemistry department's request for a second fume-cupboard laboratory on cost grounds. The head of chemistry, who argued strongly for it, was not at the meeting. Your communications plan makes you responsible for telling requesters the outcome of their requests. Minutes normally go to all departments within five working days. She presents to the university council on Friday. It is Tuesday. What should you do?

options.text: Ask the board's secretary to circulate the minutes early, by tomorrow, so that the head of chemistry and the other departments all hear the decision through the official record.
options.rationale: The candidate gets the speed right but chooses the wrong medium. A disappointing decision arriving in minutes alongside everyone else gives her no chance to ask why, and invites the reaction you most want to avoid.

options.text: Contact the head of chemistry today to tell her the decision and the reasons for it, and explain how she can respond if she wants to ask the board to reconsider.
