options.rationale: She hears it first, from the person responsible for telling her, in time to adjust her council presentation. A conversation lets her ask questions, and explaining the route to reconsideration keeps the process open to her.

options.text: Ask the board's chair to phone the head of chemistry, since a decision of this weight is better delivered by the person who chaired the board that took it.
options.rationale: The plan gives this task to you. Passing it upward because the news is unwelcome adds a step, may not reach her before Friday, and makes the chair carry a communication that is yours to make.

options.text: Email the head of chemistry today with the decision and a copy of the cost analysis the board considered, so that she has the facts in writing before her council presentation.
options.rationale: This is timely and complete, but it delivers an unwelcome outcome to someone who fought for the opposite in a medium that allows no exchange. A conversation first, followed by the papers, gives her the facts and the chance to respond.

questions.explanation: A stakeholder with a direct stake in a decision should hear an unwelcome outcome promptly and personally, before it reaches them through formal distribution or from others, and in a medium that lets them ask questions. Timing matters most when they are about to act on the old assumption, and the formal record then confirms what they already know rather than breaking the news.
questions.mindset: People should hear bad news about their own requests first, directly, and in a conversation.

questions.stem: On an airport baggage-handling replacement, two steering group members disputed at this month's meeting what had been decided last month about the commissioning sequence. Last month's minutes were circulated 19 days after the meeting as eight pages of narrative, and neither member had commented on them. Work has already started on the basis of one interpretation. Which two actions should you take to prevent this happening again?

options.text: At the end of each meeting, have the chair read back each decision and its owner, and record them in wording the members agree before they leave the room.
options.rationale: Agreeing the wording while the discussion is fresh removes the gap in which two people's memories drift apart. Disagreement surfaces in the meeting, where it can be settled, rather than weeks later.

options.text: Circulate a decisions and actions log within one working day of each meeting, separate from the narrative minutes, and ask members to flag any errors within a set period.
options.rationale: A short, prompt log makes decisions easy to find and check. Asking for corrections within a set window turns silence into informed acceptance instead of a sign that nobody read eight pages.

options.text: Record future steering meetings, with the members' agreement, so that any later dispute about what was decided can be settled by playing back the relevant discussion.
options.rationale: A recording is complete but not clear. Disputes are usually about interpretation rather than words spoken, and searching hours of audio after work has started moves the effort to the worst possible moment.

options.text: Ask the two members to agree between themselves which interpretation is correct, and update last month's minutes to reflect whatever they agree as the record.
options.rationale: The current dispute does need settling, but the question asks how to prevent recurrence. The decision also belonged to the whole group, so two members cannot redefine it between themselves.

options.text: Expand the minutes to set out the discussion leading to each decision in more detail, so that the reasoning behind every decision is clear to readers who look back later.
options.rationale: The candidate treats the problem as too little detail. Longer narrative makes decisions harder to find and less likely to be read, which is how the disagreement went unnoticed for a month.

questions.explanation: A record of a decision is useful only if the decision-makers agree its wording while the discussion is fresh and can find it easily later. Confirming decisions aloud before a meeting ends, and circulating a short decisions log quickly with a window for corrections, closes the gap in which memories diverge and work starts on different interpretations.
questions.mindset: Agree what was decided before people leave the room, and write it down where it can be found.

questions.stem: Your agile team builds farm management software. The product owner is the only person who talks to farmers; she writes detailed stories from her interviews and passes them to the developers. Over three sprints, two features were built exactly as written but rejected by farmers at review because they did not fit how work is done in the field. The product owner plans to write even more detailed stories. Which two actions should you take?

options.text: Support the product owner in adding more detail to each story, with screen mock-ups and step-by-step workflows, so that less is left to the developers' interpretation.
options.rationale: The features were built exactly as written, so interpretation was not the failure. More detail amplifies one person's understanding of the field and makes the hand-off longer without making it richer.

options.text: Arrange for developers to join some of the product owner's farm visits, so that they see at first hand the work the features have to support and can ask farmers questions.
options.rationale: Context that never reaches a story is what the rejected features lacked. Seeing the work and talking to farmers gives developers understanding no document can carry, and shortens the path the need travels.

options.text: Ask farmers to review and sign off each story in writing before it is accepted into a sprint, so that requirements are confirmed by the people who will use the features.
options.rationale: The candidate adds a written gate. Farmers approving text they read away from the field are unlikely to spot the mismatch, and sign-off turns stories into contracts while slowing the flow of work.

options.text: Hold refinement sessions where the product owner and developers work through concrete examples of farm tasks together before stories are accepted into a sprint.
options.rationale: Talking through specific examples exposes gaps in shared understanding before anything is built. It replaces a one-way document hand-off with a conversation in which developers can test their assumptions.

options.text: Ask the product owner to record her farmer interviews and share the recordings with the developers, so that they can hear users' needs directly without extra travel.
options.rationale: Recordings give raw material but no chance to ask questions, and the interviews are still framed by the product owner's questions. Developers rarely find time to watch hours of them, so the channel stays one-way in practice.

questions.explanation: Every hand-off between the people who understand a need and the people who build for it loses context, and adding detail to the hand-off document does not restore what was lost. Shortening the path, by putting builders in contact with users and their setting and by replacing documents with conversation about concrete examples, builds a shared understanding that a written story can only remind people of.
questions.mindset: Shorten the path between the people who need something and the people who build it.

questions.stem: Your hybrid project is replacing a publisher's editorial system. For a week, team members have been saying that the project is about to be cancelled, after the sponsor was seen in long meetings with finance. Two contractors have started looking for other work. You know the board is reviewing all capital projects, that no decision has been made, and that the outcome is due in three weeks. Which two actions should you take?

options.text: Ask the sponsor today what you may say about the review, and when the team can expect to hear more about its outcome directly from her.
options.rationale: You know the review exists, but the sponsor decides what can be shared about it. Asking today gets agreement quickly enough to answer the rumour before more people act on it.

options.text: Hold a team meeting this week to say what is and is not known about the review and when the next update will come, and take questions openly.
options.rationale: Rumour fills an information gap. Stating plainly what is known, what is not, and when more will be known replaces speculation with something accurate without promising an outcome.

options.text: Reassure the team that the project is valued and that you expect it to continue, so that the contractors do not leave before the review is concluded.
options.rationale: The candidate offers comfort in place of information. You do not know the outcome, and if the project is cut your credibility goes with it at the moment the team most needs to trust you.

options.text: Say nothing to the team until the board's decision is known, so that people are not given partial information that may later turn out to be wrong.
options.rationale: Waiting for certainty feels responsible, but three weeks of silence lets the rumour harden. Partial information that is accurate and labelled as partial is better than none.

options.text: Speak privately to the two contractors about their plans, and offer them contract extensions to keep them on the project until the review's outcome is known.
options.rationale: This targets the most visible symptom and commits money during a review of whether the money will be spent. The rest of the team still hears nothing, so the rumour keeps working on them.

questions.explanation: Rumour moves faster than an official update that waits for certainty. Stating what is known, what is not, and when more will be known, after agreeing with the decision owner what can be shared, gives people something accurate to act on without promising an outcome nobody has decided. Silence and reassurance both leave the gap for speculation to fill.
questions.mindset: Fill an information vacuum with what you know and when you will know more, not with reassurance.

questions.stem: Stakeholders of an agile team building a hotel booking engine keep asking the team the same kinds of question. Match each question to the information radiator that answers it most directly. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: The commercial director asks whether everything planned for the summer release is likely to be finished by its June date.
The operations manager wants to see where work is piling up between development, testing and deployment.
A revenue manager wants to know whether her rate-parity feature is near enough the top to be built in the next couple of sprints.

options.text: Release burn-up chart
options.rationale: A release burn-up plots completed work against the total scope of the release over time, so the trend line shows whether the June scope is likely to be reached and makes scope growth visible too.

options.text: Cumulative flow diagram
options.rationale: A cumulative flow diagram shows how much work sits in each stage over time. A band that widens marks the stage where work is accumulating, which is exactly the operations manager's question.

options.text: Ordered product backlog
options.rationale: Position in the ordered backlog, read against the team's typical throughput, tells her roughly when her feature will be reached. No chart answers a question about relative priority as directly.

options.text: Sprint burndown chart
options.rationale: Not used. A sprint burndown shows remaining work in the current sprint only, so it says nothing about the release date, where work queues between stages, or what comes next.

questions.explanation: Each information radiator is built to answer a particular question, and stakeholders get the clearest answer when they are pointed to the one designed for theirs. Release progress is a question about scope against time, flow problems are a question about work by stage, and 'when will mine be done' is a question about order. Sending people to the wrong artefact produces either confusion or a confident misreading.
questions.mindset: Point a stakeholder to the artefact built to answer their question.

questions.stem: On a rail depot redevelopment, several messages need to be delivered this week. Match each message to the person best placed to deliver it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Explaining to the client organisation's staff why the board has decided to cancel the project's second phase and redirect its budget.
Telling the scaffolding crew, before tomorrow's shift, about a revised tie-in sequence after a design check found the old one unsafe.
Telling an individual engineer that her assignment to the project will end early because the second phase has been cancelled.

options.text: The project sponsor
options.rationale: A strategic decision about the business case is best explained by the person who owns it. Staff can ask the sponsor why, and hear the answer from someone with the standing to give it.

options.text: The crew's site supervisor
options.rationale: The supervisor directs the crew's daily work and briefs them at the start of each shift. A safety-critical change lands best through the person whose instructions they already follow on site.

options.text: The engineer's line manager
options.rationale: News about someone's role belongs with the person responsible for their employment and next assignment. The line manager can answer the questions that follow, which the project cannot.

options.text: The project communications officer
options.rationale: Not used. A communications officer can help shape and schedule broad messages, but each of these depends on the authority or relationship of the sender, which a communications role does not hold.

questions.explanation: Who delivers a message shapes how it is received as much as what it says. Strategic decisions carry most weight from the person accountable for them, operational instructions from the person who directs the work, and personal news from the person responsible for the individual. Choosing the sender is part of planning the communication, not an afterthought.
questions.mindset: Choose the messenger whose authority or relationship the message depends on.

questions.stem: On a hybrid programme moving a building society's mortgage platform to the cloud, the project manager is choosing how to communicate in several situations. Complete each sentence with the form of communication that fits best. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Notifying the cloud supplier that it has missed a contractual service milestone, which triggers the service-credit clause, calls for
Checking with a developer, mid-sprint, what she meant by a comment on an acceptance criterion that two testers have read in opposite ways, calls for
Presenting the case for a revised go-live window to the programme board so that it can take a decision, calls for

options.text: formal written communication
options.rationale: A contractual notice with financial consequences needs a formal, written, traceable form that the contract will recognise. Anything less invites a dispute about whether notice was ever given.

options.text: informal verbal communication
options.rationale: Clarifying meaning is fastest in a quick conversation, where the developer can explain and the PM can check understanding at once. Two opposite readings show that another written exchange is likely to miss.

options.text: formal verbal communication
options.rationale: A presentation to a decision-making board is formal and spoken: structured, prepared and delivered to people who need to question it before deciding, usually backed by a paper.

options.text: informal written communication
options.rationale: Not used. Quick emails and chat messages suit low-stakes updates that benefit from a light record. The notice needs formality, the clarification needs conversation, and the board needs a prepared presentation.

questions.explanation: Two choices shape most communication: how formal it must be, which follows from consequence and audience, and whether it is written or spoken, which follows from whether a record or an exchange matters more. Contractual and governance matters lean formal; clearing up meaning leans verbal, because conversation lets understanding be checked in real time.
questions.mindset: Decide how formal and how interactive a message must be before choosing how to send it.

questions.stem: An agile product has three teams. Team Manila works 01:00–09:30 UTC, team Lisbon 08:00–16:30 UTC, and team Denver 15:00–23:30 UTC. The product owner wants one weekly live session in which all three teams review the increment together, held within everyone's working hours.

blanks.label: Hours of shared working time between Manila and Lisbon each day
blanks.rationale: Manila finishes at 09:30 UTC and Lisbon starts at 08:00 UTC, so they overlap from 08:00 to 09:30: 1.5 hours.

blanks.label: Hours of shared working time between Lisbon and Denver each day
blanks.rationale: Lisbon finishes at 16:30 UTC and Denver starts at 15:00 UTC, so they overlap from 15:00 to 16:30: 1.5 hours.

blanks.label: Hours of shared working time when all three teams are at work
blanks.rationale: Manila has finished by 09:30 UTC and Denver does not start until 15:00 UTC, so there is no moment when all three are working: 0 hours.

blanks.label: Which team shares working hours with both of the others — name its city
blanks.rationale: Lisbon overlaps Manila in the morning UTC and Denver in the afternoon UTC, so it is the only team that can talk live to both, which makes it the natural relay for anything the other two need to share.

questions.explanation: Work out when people can actually talk before designing how they will. Where no shared window exists, a single live event either pushes one team permanently out of hours or has to be redesigned: rotate the inconvenience fairly, relay through the team that overlaps both, or move the review to an asynchronous format such as a recorded demonstration with written feedback.
questions.mindset: Map when people can actually talk before deciding how they will.

questions.stem: You are building a vaccine fill-finish facility. The site's licence requires the regulator to be notified within five working days of any deviation affecting a validated system. The diagram shows five rows of the project's communications matrix. Select the row that will cause the project to breach an obligation stated here.

graphic.title: Five rows of a communications matrix: audience, content, owner and timing
graphic.caption: Select a row. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between rows, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Sponsor: monthly dashboard on cost, schedule and risks, issued by the project manager on the first Monday
regions.rationale: Monthly is slow for a regulator but no timing obligation to the sponsor is stated. Choosing this row reacts to the lowest frequency on the page rather than reading it against the obligation in the stem.

regions.label: Quality head: each deviation reported to her by the validation lead on the day it is found, and logged
regions.rationale: This row works: the person who will notify the regulator learns of a deviation the same day. The candidate mistakes the internal step for the external one, when this step gives the most time possible.

regions.label: Regulator: deviation notifications sent by the quality head once the deviation is approved at the monthly change board
regions.rationale: The trigger is the flaw. Tying the notice to a board that meets monthly means a deviation found just after a meeting waits around four weeks, far beyond five working days, however quickly the quality head acts afterwards.

regions.label: Commissioning contractors: daily 07:30 briefing on validated-system status, led by the site supervisor
regions.rationale: A daily briefing is the most frequent channel in the matrix and meets any need for timely site information. Choosing it confuses the audience nearest the validated systems with the one the licence names.

regions.label: Site neighbours: quarterly newsletter on construction traffic and noise, posted by the community liaison officer
regions.rationale: Quarterly may be too seldom for some neighbours, but the stem states no obligation to them. The candidate judges the row on general good practice instead of against the obligation given.

questions.explanation: A communications matrix is tested by reading each row against the obligations it must meet, and the timing of a row is set by its trigger as much as by its frequency. A notification tied to an internal event that happens on a slower cycle, such as an approval board, inherits that cycle's delay. Check what starts each communication, not only how often it runs.
questions.mindset: Check what triggers a communication, not just how often it is sent.
